# U.S. Unemployment Rate Forecasting Pipeline

## Overview
This project implements an end-to-end forecasting pipeline for predicting the U.S. unemployment rate one month ahead. Economic data is retrieved from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), transformed into model features, and used by an ensemble of a Ridge Regression model and a persistence model. Forecasts, model outputs, and actual values after release are stored in a SQLite database.

The pipeline checks FRED for newly released observations and generates a new forecast when updated data becomes available. This creates an ex-ante collection of forecasts over time, enabling the model’s predictions to be evaluated against unemployment rates released after each forecast was made.

## Installation and Setup

### How to Download this Repository from GitHub

The repository can either be directly downloaded as a `.zip` from GitHub or be cloned to your current directory via the terminal:

```
git clone https://github.com/mx-lnk/us-unemployment-forecast

cd us-unemployment-forecast
```



### How to Install All Necessary Python Packages

All Python packages are listed in the `requirements.txt`.

    Open a terminal in the project directory or navigate to it using `cd`.

#### Create a virtual environment (optional but recommended)
Create a virtual environment named `newvenv` or any name of your choice

```
python -m venv newvenv
```
Then activate this virtual environment. Do not forget to replace `newvenv` with whatever name you have chosen.

**Windows:**
```
newvenv\Scripts\activate
```
**macOS / Linux**
```
source newvenv/bin/activate
```

#### Install all packages listed in requirements.txt

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
```


### Running the Pipeline

The entire pipeline can be executed by running:
```
python src/main.py
```

If it is executed for the first time it will set up the database, populate it with data from the FRED API, and create and store its first forecast. Whenever you run it again, it will only continue if a new data set is available on FRED. This behavior can be overridden by setting the parameter `force_execution = True` for the `init_pipeline` function.

The forecasts and their metrics are stored in the SQLite database under `data/us_unemployment.db`. All forecasts are stored in the `Runs` table, regardless of whether execution was forced. The `Forecast` table contains the most recent run of each month and represents the ex-ante collection of forecasts.

A quick way to produce standalone forecasts and view them as a Pandas DataFrame is to execute the model in `notebooks/model.ipynb`. For this to work, first run python `src/main.py` to set up the database and provide the required input data.

#### Logging

Pipeline executions are logged to `logs/main_pipeline.log`. The log records major pipeline stages, skipped executions when no new data is available, and errors encountered during execution.

Log files are automatically rotated to prevent them from growing indefinitely. The `logs/` directory is created automatically and is excluded from version control.


### How to Get and Add an API Key

You can request an API key directly by creating an account on the [FRED website](https://fredaccount.stlouisfed.org/login/secure/). Creating an account and using the API is completely free. After having created an account you can request and view your API keys by visiting the [*API Keys* section](https://fredaccount.stlouisfed.org/apikeys) under your account.

Once you have obtained your API key, run
```
cp .env.example .env
```
to create a `.env` based on the template. Afterward open the `.env` file and paste your API key between the quotation marks.

## Project Structure

```
src/        Core pipeline and model code
sql/        SQLite queries and schema
notebooks/  Exploration and model development
data/       SQLite database
logs/       Rotating logs about main.py
```

The above depicted pipeline works as follows:

1. Observations and metadata for the series IDs of the target and the features will be requested from the FRED API.
2. The data will be split into observations and metadata, and then stored in their respective tables in the SQLite database.
3. All observations will be requested from the database, processed into a feature set and a target set, and then converted into a DataFrame.
4. This DataFrame is fed into the Ridge-Persistence ensemble model, which returns three DataFrames: a test results DataFrame containing predictions from the test period, a test metrics DataFrame containing evaluation metrics and the training and testing periods, and a forecast DataFrame containing the production forecast and its training period.
5. Everything except the test results DataFrame is stored in the SQLite database.
6.  When the actual value of the forecasted period is released, this value will be added to the database for error tracking.

## Data
### Data Sources
All data is requested via the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) API, provided by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Observations and metadata are requested for these series IDs:

### About the Requested Data
The requested data sets can be identified on FRED via their series ID. All requested series IDs follow a monthly release schedule. The following table contains all requested series IDs: 
<table>
    <thead>
        <tr>
            <th>Series ID</th>
            <th>Name</th>
        </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td>INDPRO</td>
            <td>Industrial Production: Total Index</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td>JTSJOL</td>
            <td>Job Openings: Total Nonfarm</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td>UNRATE</td>
            <td>Unemployment Rate</td>
        </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

>[!note] Requested Time Periods
> Data is requested starting one month before the earliest common observation date of the series listed above to accommodate the lagged features.
### Where the Data Is Stored
All data requested from FRED or generated by the pipeline is stored in a SQLite database located in `data/`. The directory and database are created automatically and excluded from version control.

### How Data Gets Updated
Whenever the pipeline gets triggered (either naturally or through a forced execution), all observations and metadata will be updated to incorporate any revisions. If not forced, the pipeline will only execute when a new complete data set for all series IDs has been published on FRED. 

## Feature Engineering
The U.S. unemployment rate of next month ($UNRATE_{t+1}$) is predicted by these features:

- $INDPRO_{t-1}$
- $\log_{10}(JTSJOL_{t-1})$
- $UNRATE_t$

>[!Note] Real time vs published time
> The current time $t$ refers to the current month of UNRATE being published on FRED. The Federal Reserve publishes the unemployment rate with approximately a one-month delay relative to real time.

### Feature Selection Process
All potential candidates for the feature set were initially chosen based on their economic relevance to unemployment. In the early stages of this project, three additional series IDs (PAYEMS, ICSA, CCSA) were considered but later dropped due to their unsatisfactory performance during exploratory analysis and testing in an early version of the model. The three retained series IDs showed meaningful correlations with the unemployment rate, although the strength of these relationships varied across the features. The scatter plots were additionally used to visually examine the relationships and the effect of different transformations.

After the exploratory analysis, the three retained series IDs were bundled into different feature sets, varying in their composition and whether $\log_{10}$ transformations were applied. The candidate feature sets were compared based on their validation performance, and the feature set with the lowest validation MAE was selected as the final feature set.

Note that the INDPRO and JTSJOL features are lagged by one month to account for their later release relative to UNRATE.


### Feature Processing
All features are sorted in ascending chronological order. Time lagged features are shifted one month down and the target of $UNRATE_{t+1}$ is shifted one month up, so that they align with time $t$. Additionally, $\log_{10}$ is applied to JTSJOL.

### Missing Values
Rows with missing values will be dropped. Imputation is intentionally avoided for two reasons. First, it could introduce look-ahead leakage within the current backtesting implementation. Second, between December 2000 and August 2026, only one missing value occurred.


## The Model
The model in its current form is a Ridge-Regression-Persistence-Ensemble model.

### Reasoning behind the Model Selection
The exploratory analysis revealed correlations between the features. Ridge Regression was chosen as a regularized linear model because its L2 penalty can reduce coefficient sensitivity when predictors contain overlapping information.

Additionally, the final model is an ensemble of Ridge Regression and a persistence model, due to the persistence model’s strong performance as a baseline.

### Technical Implementation
The model was implemented using NumPy and Pandas rather than pre-built machine learning libraries such as scikit-learn. This was done intentionally to provide greater transparency into the underlying implementation and to gain a deeper understanding of the model.

### Ridge Regression

Ridge Regression extends ordinary least squares by adding an L2 penalty to the cost function:

$$
\min_{\beta}
\left[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2
\right]
$$

where $\lambda$ controls the strength of the regularization. A larger $\lambda$ results in stronger coefficient shrinkage, while $\lambda = 0$ reduces the model to ordinary least squares.

For this model, $\lambda$ is not fixed manually but selected based on validation performance.

### Persistence Model

The persistence model serves as the baseline and assumes that next month’s unemployment rate will remain equal to the current month’s unemployment rate:

$$
\hat{y}_{t+1}^{P}=y_t
$$

Despite its simplicity, persistence provides a strong baseline for the unemployment rate and performed competitively during model development.

### Ensemble Model

The final forecast combines the Ridge Regression forecast with the persistence forecast:

$$
\hat{y}_{t+1} = w\hat{y}_{t+1}^{Ridge} + (1-w)\hat{y}_{t+1}^{P}
$$

where $w$ determines the contribution of the Ridge Regression model. The ensemble weight is selected based on validation performance.

### Training and Validation

To preserve the chronological structure of the time series, the data is split sequentially rather than randomly. The first 60% of observations are used for training, the following 20% for validation, and the remaining 20% as the final test set.

The validation period is used to select the feature set, the Ridge penalty $\lambda$, and the ensemble weight $w$. After the model configuration has been selected, the Ridge model is refitted on the combined training and validation data before being evaluated on the test period.

Model performance is evaluated using MAE, RMSE and MAPE and compared with the persistence baseline.

## Results and Evaluation
The final model was evaluated on the holdout test period from July 2021 to July 2026. Its performance was compared against the persistence baseline model.

The ensemble model outperforms the persistence baseline model in all three metrics. As the MAE indicates, the ensemble model's forecasts differ approximately 0.09 percentage points on average from the actual observed unemployment rate.

Additionally, the larger improvement in RMSE compared with MAE indicates that the ensemble model also reduced some of the larger forecast errors relative to the persistence baseline model.

## Limitations and Areas for Future Improvements
The forecasting pipeline has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting its results.

### Revised Historical Data when Backtesting
The historical data used for model training and backtesting is retrieved from FRED and may contain revisions that were made after the original observations were first published. While the feature pipeline accounts for differences in publication timing by lagging INDPRO and JTSJOL, it does not reconstruct the exact data vintage that would have been available at each historical forecast date.

As a result, the backtest should not be interpreted as a fully real-time historical simulation. A more rigorous implementation could use vintage data from ALFRED to reconstruct the information set available at each forecast origin.

### Limited Feature Set
The model intentionally uses a relatively small number of economic indicators. While this keeps the model simple and interpretable, other variables containing useful information about future unemployment are not considered.

### Model Specification
Ridge Regression assumes a linear relationship between the transformed features and the target. The exploratory analysis indicates that some relationships in the data are more complex, meaning that the model may not capture all nonlinear dynamics.

### Structural Changes
Relationships between labor-market and economic indicators are not necessarily stable over time. Events such as recessions, the COVID-19 pandemic, policy changes, or changes in labor-market structure can therefore reduce the usefulness of relationships learned from historical observations.
